\chapter{Four Core Colours}
\label{ch:te-core-colours}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name four basic colours in Telugu — black, white, red, and blue.}

Say \te{నలుపు}, \te{తెలుపు}, \te{ఎరుపు} — Telugu's own three — then \te{నీలం}, blue, which Telugu borrowed rather than inherited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nalupu telupu erupu nīlam]{\te{నలుపు}, \te{తెలుపు}, \te{ఎరుపు}, \te{నీలం} — the pattern completes itself}

\label{lesson:TE-C11-rangulu}



\begin{quote}
By now the shape should feel familiar: native colors for black, white, and red — and one shared Sanskrit word for blue. Telugu confirms it a fourth time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Three native colors}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నలుపు}} (\emph{nalupu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{black}\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian.
  \item \textbf{\te{తెలుపు}} (\emph{telupu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{white}\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian.
  \item \textbf{\te{ఎరుపు}} (\emph{erupu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{red}\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{నీలం}} (\emph{nīlam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{blue}\textquotedblright{} — the identical Sanskrit \textbf{\te{నీల}} (\emph{nīla}) loan that also sits in Tamil (\emph{nīlam}), Malayalam (\emph{nīla}), Kannada (\emph{nīli}), and Hindi (\emph{nīlā}). Four Dravidian languages plus Hindi, all independently keeping their own native black/white/red, and all reaching for the \textbf{exact same} borrowed word the moment it comes to blue.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nalupu, telupu, erupu\textquotedblright{} — black, white, red
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nīlam\textquotedblright{} — blue, the word the four Dravidian languages and Hindi all share
  \item the whole pattern, one more time — native, native, native, \textbf{borrowed}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What's the pattern across Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, and Telugu's basic colors? (\textbf{Black, white, and red are native Dravidian words in every one of them; blue is a shared Sanskrit loan (nīla) in every one of them.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\te{◌ె} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S115-vowel-sign-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ల} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{◌ూ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ె}}
\textbf{\te{◌ె}} — \emph{e}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{e}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ె} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} \emph{veḷḷu} — to go (and \te{వచ్చు}, to come)
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}} \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} — 'I know Telugu'
  \item \textbf{\te{ఒకటి} \te{రెండు} \te{మూడు} \te{నాలుగు} \te{ఐదు}} \emph{okaṭi reṇḍu mūḍu nālugu aidu} — one to five
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ె} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ె} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ె} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{వెళ్ళు}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ె} three times, saying \emph{e} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ె} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ె}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{e} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.

One more, from much earlier: \te{౭} — what amount does it stand for?
\end{tcolorbox}
